steps.text: Write the introduction for a theory paper on fair division of multi-layered cakes (fairly sharing several time-scheduled facilities among agents). steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In our daily lives there are many cases of time scheduling where we arrange our schedules so we can finish our daily tasks. Think of a group of university students who want to enjoy several facilities, like a seminar lecture or an indoor game. The two facilities open and close at the same hours. Everyone in the group wants to enjoy both facilities, but each student has a different preferred time period for each one.

Put simply, the problem of dividing a cake is a metaphor for how to divide a resource that can be shared among n agents with different preferences in a fair way. The cake-cutting problem is a central topic in the theory of fair division, and it has got a lot of attention in mathematics, economics, political science, and computer science. Giving each agent a fair share of the cake is hard. The most important criteria for a fair allocation in the cake-cutting literature are envy-freeness and proportionality. In an envy-free allocation, every agent is pleased with the pieces they get compared to the allocation of any other agent. In a proportional allocation, each agent gets at least \frac{1}{n} of the value he estimates for the cake. If all of the cake is divided, envy-freeness implies proportionality. It is known that envy-free allocations always exist, even if each agent has to receive a connected piece. Besides existence, the algorithmic design side has also been studied for a long time. We can compute a proportional allocation and also an envy-free allocation for any number of agents.

- Multi-layered
  - example not plain cake cutting: divide the two time intervals independently, no overlaps
  - Hosseini et al. initiate multi-layered cake cutting
  - facility = divisible heterogeneous layer; additive valuation over disjoint (non-overlapping) intervals
  - feasible = no overlapping intervals; contiguous = one contiguous interval per facility
  - goal: fair, feasible, contiguous multi-allocations

## 1.1 Our results

- section 3: exact feasible multi-allocation, two agents, Austin-moving knife
- section 4: proportional feasible contiguous for three layers, n\geq 3 agents; also 2^{a}3 layers, n\geq 2^{a}3 agents, a\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}

## 1.2 Related Work

- cake cutting widely studied in economics, mathematics, CS
- Hosseini et al.: two layers, three agents, two types of preferences
- Igarashi and Meunier: prime power agents, layers at most agents, combinatorial topology
- papers where agents benefit from all pieces with no constraints

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In our daily lives there are many cases of time scheduling where we arrange our schedules so we can finish our daily tasks. Think of a group of university students who want to enjoy several facilities, like a seminar lecture or an indoor game. The two facilities open and close at the same hours. Everyone in the group wants to enjoy both facilities, but each student has a different preferred time period for each one.

Put simply, the problem of dividing a cake is a metaphor for how to divide a resource that can be shared among n agents with different preferences in a fair way. The cake-cutting problem is a central topic in the theory of fair division, and it has got a lot of attention in mathematics, economics, political science, and computer science. Giving each agent a fair share of the cake is hard. The most important criteria for a fair allocation in the cake-cutting literature are envy-freeness and proportionality. In an envy-free allocation, every agent is pleased with the pieces they get compared to the allocation of any other agent. In a proportional allocation, each agent gets at least \frac{1}{n} of the value he estimates for the cake. If all of the cake is divided, envy-freeness implies proportionality. It is known that envy-free allocations always exist, even if each agent has to receive a connected piece. Besides existence, the algorithmic design side has also been studied for a long time. We can compute a proportional allocation and also an envy-free allocation for any number of agents.

But the problem of getting several facilities in the example above cannot be considered a cake-cutting problem. We have to divide the two time intervals independently so each agent can enjoy both facilities. So the question is how to fairly divide the time interval of each facility according to their preferences. Then every student can enjoy every facility, and the time intervals allotted for each facility never overlap. With these constraints, Hosseini et al. initiate the multi-layered cake cutting problem. In the multi-layered cake cutting problem we see how to solve this problem. We consider each facility as a divisible heterogeneous layer of a multi-layered cake. Every student has an additive preference, called valuation, over disjoint (non-overlapping) intervals. The valuation of the same part of the cake can be very different for different students. A division of a multi-layered cake is feasible if no student's time intervals contain overlapping intervals. The division is contiguous if each student gets a contiguous time interval for each facility. In multi-layered cake cutting our goal is to find multi-allocations that are fair and also meet the feasibility and contiguity constraints.

## 1.1 Our results

In section 3 we use the idea of the Austin-moving knife procedure to show that an exact feasible multi-allocation exists for two agents. In section 4 we show that a proportional multi-allocation that is feasible and contiguous exists for three layers and any number n\geq 3 of agents. We also prove that a proportional multi-allocation that is feasible and contiguous exists for 2^{a}3 layers and for n\geq 2^{a}3 agents, where a\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.

## 1.2 Related Work

The cake cutting problem is the central topic in fair division. It has been studied a lot in recent years in the economics, mathematics, and computer science literature. Hosseini et al. initiate the study of multi-layered cake cutting in order to fairly divide multiple divisible resources among a group of agents. They show that an envy-free multi-allocation that is feasible and contiguous exists for two layers and three agents with two types of preferences. Igarashi and Meunier also show, using combinatorial topology, that there is an envy-free multi-allocation that is feasible and contiguous when the number of agents is a prime power and the number of layers is at most the number of agents. A few papers are most related to multi-layered cake cutting, where agents can benefit from all allocated pieces at the same time with no constraints.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
There are several instances of time scheduling in our daily lives where we arrange our schedules so that we can finish our daily tasks. Consider a group of university students who want to enjoy several facilities, such as a seminar lecture or an indoor game. The two facilities have the same opening and closing hours. Everyone in the group is willing to enjoy both facilities, but each has a distinct preferred time period for each one. In simple terms, the problem of dividing a cake is a metaphor for how to divide a resource that can be shared among n agents with different preferences in a fair way. The cake-cutting problem is a central topic in the theory of fair division [1,2,3,4], and it has received significant attention in the domains of mathematics, economics, political science, and computer science [5,6,7,8,9,10]. It is hard to give each agent a fair share of the cake. Envy-freeness and proportionality are the most important criteria for a fair allocation in the cake-cutting literature. In an envy-free allocation, every agent is pleased with the pieces they are allocated as opposed to any other agent’s allocation. In a proportional allocation, each agent receives at least \frac{1}{n} of the value he estimates for the cake. When all of the cake has been divided, envy-freeness entails proportionality. It is well known that envy-free allocations always exist [11], even if we require that each agent receive a connected piece [12,13]. Beyond existence, the algorithmic design aspect has also been considered for a long time [14,15,16,17,18,19]. For any number of agents, we can calculate a proportional allocation as well as an envy-free allocation. However, we cannot consider the problem of getting several facilities in the example above to be a cake-cutting problem. We have to divide the two time intervals independently so that each agent can enjoy both facilities. The issue now is how to fairly divide each facility’s time interval according to their preferences, so that every student can enjoy every facility and the allotted time intervals for each facility never overlap. Adopting these constraints, Hosseini et al. [20] initiate the multi-layered cake cutting problem, in which we see how to solve this problem. We consider each facility as a divisible heterogeneous layer of a multi-layered cake. Every student has an additive preference, called valuation, over disjoint (non-overlapping) intervals. Note that different students can value the same part of the cake very differently. A division of a multi-layered cake is feasible if no student’s time intervals contain overlapping intervals. The division is contiguous if each student gets a contiguous time interval for each facility. Our goal in multi-layered cake cutting is to find multi-allocations that are fair while also meeting the constraints of feasibility and contiguity.

## 1.1 Our results

In section 3, we show the existence of an exact feasible multi-allocation for two agents using the idea of the Austin-moving knife procedure. In section 4, we show that there exists a proportional multi-allocation that is feasible and contiguous for three layers and any number n\geq 3 of agents. We also prove the existence of a proportional multi-allocation that is feasible and contiguous for 2^{a}3 layers and for n\geq 2^{a}3 agents, where a\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.

## 1.2 Related Work

The cake cutting problem is the central topic in fair division. In recent years, it has been extensively studied in the economics, mathematics, and computer science literature [21,22,23,24,25]. To fairly divide multiple divisible resources among a group of agents, Hosseini et al. [20] initiate the study of multi-layered cake cutting. They show that there exists an envy-free multi-allocation that is feasible and contiguous for two layers and three agents with two types of preferences. Igarashi and Meunier [26] also show, using combinatorial topology, that an envy-free multi-allocation exists that is feasible and contiguous when the number of agents is a prime power and the number of layers is at most the number of agents. A few papers are most related to multi-layered cake cutting, where agents can simultaneously benefit from all allocated pieces with no constraints [27,28,29].
